hints: Count carbons, hydrogens, nitrogens, oxygens and sulfurs separately from the Sunset Yellow anion diagram, remembering the two benzene type rings share no atoms and the $\text{OH}$ hydrogen counts.
walkthrough:
Break the anion into fragments to count**
Look at the picture with me. Left side is a disubstituted benzene, so that is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}$. Middle is an azo link, $-\text{N}=\text{N}-$, so that is $\text{N}_{2}$. Right side is a trisubstituted naphthalene, $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{5}$, plus one $\text{OH}$ group.

Add oxygens, sulfurs and charge**
Each $-\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ contributes $\text{S}_{1}\text{O}_{3}$. Two of them give $\text{S}_{2}\text{O}_{6}$. Add the one O from $\text{OH}$ to get $\text{O}_{7}$. Hydrogens are $4 + 5 + 1 = 10$. Carbons are $6 + 10 = 16$. The two sulfonate groups give an overall $2-$ charge.

hints: Split the $\text{N}=\text{N}$ bond in the product in your mind, the left benzene fragment must come from E and F, the right naphthalene fragment must come from G.
Recall that an aromatic amine $\text{Ar-NH}_{2}$ is converted to a diazonium ion $\text{Ar-N}_{2}^{+}$ in step 1, so work out what E must lose and what F must gain.

Use the given formulae $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{SC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{NH}_{2}$ and $\text{HOC}_{10}\text{H}_{6}\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ and the para substitution pattern visible in the product to place the substituents.
walkthrough:
See this as a classic azo dye puzzle**
You have a coloured $\text{Ar-N=N-Ar'}$ molecule. It is always made from a diazonium ion plus a phenol or naphthol. The $\text{N}=\text{N}$ bridge is the join. Everything left of it comes from one starting material, everything right of it comes from the other.

Assign E from the left half**
The left half of Sunset Yellow is $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}-$. The formula of E is $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{SC}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{NH}_{2}$. That fits perfectly if E is 4-aminobenzenesulfonate. Draw a benzene with $\text{NH}_{2}$ at the top and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ at the bottom, para to each other, exactly matching the para pattern in the product.

Assign F as the diazonium ion**
Step 1 converts an aromatic primary amine to a diazonium ion. So $-\text{NH}_{2}$ becomes $-\text{N}_{2}^{+}$. F is therefore $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-N}\equiv\text{N}^{+}$, again para disubstituted. The $-\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ group is unchanged, just a spectator that improves solubility.

Assign G from the right half**
The right half is a naphthalene bearing $\text{OH}$ and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ with the azo link ortho to the $\text{OH}$. G has formula $\text{HOC}_{10}\text{H}_{6}\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$, so it is the naphthol itself before coupling. Draw naphthalene with $\text{OH}$ at the coupling ring ortho to the position where the $\text{N}=\text{N}$ will attach, and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ on the other ring in the same position as shown in Sunset Yellow.

Final answer: E: $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-NH}_{2}$ with $\text{NH}_{2}$ and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ para to each other.
F: $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-N}_{2}^{+}$ with $\text{N}_{2}^{+}$ ($-\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^{+}$) and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ para to each other.
G: $\text{HO-C}_{10}\text{H}_{6}\text{-SO}_{3}^{-}$, 2-naphthol with $\text{OH}$ ortho to the coupling position and $\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$ on the second ring as in the product.

hints: Remember step 1 converts $\text{Ar-NH}_{2}$ to $\text{Ar-N}_{2}^{+}$, think which source of $\text{HNO}_{2}$ is used in the laboratory.
Recall why diazonium ions are kept very cold, think about their stability above $10^{\circ}\text{C}$.
For step 2 think about the conditions that convert naphthol $\text{Ar-OH}$ to the more reactive phenoxide $\text{Ar-O}^{-}$ for coupling.
walkthrough:
Make the diazonium ion in step 1**
Changing $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-NH}_{2}$ to $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-N}_{2}^{+}$ is diazotisation. In the lab you do not buy nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_{2}$, because it is unstable. You make it in situ from sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid: $$\text{NaNO}_{2} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{HNO}_{2} + \text{NaCl}$$

Keep it ice cold**
Diazonium ions decompose to give nitrogen gas if warmed, forming phenols. So you keep the mixture at $\leqslant 10^{\circ}\text{C}$, usually in an ice bath at $0$ to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$. That is a whole mark on its own, so always state the temperature for diazotisation.

Couple in alkali in step 2**
Step 2 joins the diazonium ion F to the naphthol G. Coupling to phenols and naphthols is fastest in alkaline solution where $\text{Ar-OH}$ is deprotonated to $\text{Ar-O}^{-}$, which is a much stronger electrophilic substitution partner. So use $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, high pH, still kept cold.

Final answer: step 1: $\text{NaNO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$ (or $\text{HNO}_{2}$), temperature $\leqslant 10^{\circ}\text{C}$ (0 to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$).
step 2: $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ or alkaline conditions, cold.

hints: Count chemically non-equivalent carbons, remember the left benzene has a plane of symmetry through the substituents but the naphthalene part has no symmetry.
walkthrough:
Separate symmetric from unsymmetric parts**
In carbon-13 NMR each set of equivalent carbons gives one peak. Look at the left para-disubstituted benzene: $^{-}\text{O}_{3}\text{S-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}-$. A para $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}$ has 4 distinct carbon environments because the two sides mirror each other, so 6 carbons give 4 peaks.

Add the naphthalene carbons**
The substituted naphthalene has three different substituents ($\text{OH}$, $-\text{N}=\text{N}-$, $-\text{SO}_{3}^{-}$) and no symmetry at all. All 10 carbons are in different environments, giving 10 peaks. Total $= 4 + 10 = 14$ peaks.
